tldr: We propose ACE-Ego-Hand, a method that repurposes video diffusion models as "deterministic geometry encoders" rather than image generators to rapidly recover occlusion- and out-of-sight-robust 3D bimanual trajectories from egocentric video.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of ACE-Ego-Hand. A video is compressed with a VAE and passed through a pretrained diffusion model (Wan DiT) in a single pass without noise ($\sigma=0$), extracting features from block 15. From these features, a Ray Head and a Bidirectional Spatiotemporal Decoder recover 3D hand shapes, poses, and camera-frame translations for both hands without any external detector.
overview:
Human egocentric video is a goldmine for training dexterous robot manipulation. However, recovering metric 3D hand trajectories suitable for robot learning has remained extremely difficult. Hands frequently suffer from severe occlusions during hand-object interactions, and rapid head motion often causes them to leave the frame entirely (Out of Sight: OOS). Prior methods rely on per-frame detectors or short temporal windows, which lose track of hands once they disappear and fail to maintain continuity when they reappear.

The authors turned their attention to video diffusion models (VDMs), which learn rich physical continuity and object interaction priors during pretraining. While prior works have explored diffusion models, they used round-about pipelines that perform multi-step denoising sampling to render pixel images and then estimate pose, resulting in slow inference and generative artifacts. The key insight of this work is that diffusion models are most effective when used as deterministic encoders rather than renderers.

In this work, the authors introduce ACE-Ego-Hand, a framework that runs a diffusion model with zero noise in a single forward pass as a Deterministic Clean-Latent Encoder, combining it with a bidirectional clip-level decoder and a ray-based camera solver that operates without camera intrinsics. Across five benchmarks, ACE-Ego-Hand cuts error by 30% on the occlusion-heavy ARCTIC and 40% on HOT3D, achieving 46% to 61% error reductions when out-of-sight hands are included. Furthermore, its inference speed reaches roughly 63 fps, running 33× faster than previous generative methods.
contributions: Redefining video diffusion models as deterministic feature extractors (clean-latent encoders) rather than iterative sampling generators, achieving offline clip-level 3D hand recovery without external detectors.

Proposing a Bidirectional Spatiotemporal Decoder that captures whole-clip context via bidirectional attention, combining joint-level skeleton queries with a clip-wide unique hand shape prior to smoothly interpolate and recover hands even when occluded or out of sight.

Developing a ray-based camera solver that estimates 3D viewing rays from diffusion latent representations, solving for metric positions without prior camera intrinsic calibration (focal length, etc.).
Significantly outperforming existing SOTA across five egocentric datasets, dramatically improving recovery accuracy especially for out-of-sight hand trajectories.

sections.heading: Why is egocentric hand trajectory recovery hard, and how should diffusion models be used?
sections.summary: Object occlusion and hands leaving the frame due to head motion are the biggest hurdles in recovering 3D hand trajectories from egocentric video. This paper introduces a new approach that extracts the strong physical dynamics priors of diffusion models in a single forward pass, avoiding iterative generation latency and artifacts.
sections.details:
When extracting robot imitation learning data from egocentric video, severe occlusions from hand-object interactions (HOI) and frequent out-of-sight (OOS) exits caused by rapid head motion present massive challenges.

Conventional 3D hand pose estimation methods rely on per-frame detection, cropping, or SLAM-based tracking. However, when a hand leaves the field of view even briefly, temporal context breaks, causing tracking continuity to fail upon reappearance. The authors argue that this problem is fundamentally an offline spatiotemporal reasoning task that requires examining the entire video clip at once.

Interpolating and reconstructing natural dynamics for hands out of sight requires rich priors on physics and motion. Pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs) possess such priors, but prior pipelines that run dozens of denoising steps to generate images and extract poses are extremely slow and introduce generative distortions. Additionally, direct regression in the camera frame entangles camera ego-motion with hand motion and remains tightly bound to calibrated camera intrinsics.

ACE-Ego-Hand addresses this by running a VDM in a single forward pass as a Deterministic Clean-Latent Encoder, adapting it end-to-end to 3D geometry tasks via LoRA. Coupled with a bidirectional spatiotemporal decoder and a ray-based camera solver, it enables calibration-free (K-free), smooth, metric 3D bimanual trajectory recovery even for out-of-sight hands.

sections.heading: From single-frame processing and video tracking to generative video models
sections.summary: Existing methods have mostly relied on single-frame detect-and-crop pipelines or short-window temporal models. This work aligns with representation learning that reads weight activations from video diffusion models in a single pass, offering a geometry-aware encoder free of generation overhead.
sections.details:
Prior work broadly falls into three categories:

- Single-frame hand recovery:
Many methods (such as HaMeR and WiLoR) follow a detect, crop, and regress MANO parameters pipeline. While egocentric methods incorporating camera calibration have emerged (such as WildHands and EgoForce), the limitation of relying on cropped bounding boxes remains. If a hand is heavily occluded or out of the field of view, they cannot output anything.

- Video-based hand motion recovery:
Some studies aggregate multiple frames to mitigate occlusions (OmniHands), while others use motion priors to interpolate unseen hands (GENMO, EgoH4). However, these still require per-frame detectors upstream or perform interpolation purely in a canonical pose space, failing to fully leverage the visual context of the entire video.

- Generative video models as representations:
Using video diffusion models for downstream tasks follows two paths: steering the generative process itself, or reading internal activations. Prior work like ViDiHand takes the former route, running 12 to 25 sampling steps to render geometric overlays with a frozen backbone. In contrast, this work extracts features from completely clean latents in a single forward pass and fine-tunes the backbone directly in the training loop with 3D objectives using LoRA.

sections.heading: How the deterministic diffusion encoder and bidirectional decoder work
sections.summary: The input video is passed up to block 15 of the Wan 2.2 diffusion model to extract rich features, and bidirectional attention paired with a ray-predicting camera solver simultaneously resolves joint locations, hand poses, and camera-frame translations.
sections.details:
The ACE-Ego-Hand pipeline consists of three core modules:

3.1 Generator to Encoder (Deterministic Clean-Latent Encoder):
Clean video latents at noise level $\sigma=0$ are fed into the base diffusion transformer (Wan 2.2 DiT). Computing only the first 16 blocks (up to block 15) out of 30 cuts computation roughly in half while yielding a high-quality feature grid $F$. LoRA is applied to attention and FFN layers, which are trained end-to-end alongside the patch embedding layer with 3D supervisory signals, transforming general video features into geometry-aware representations.

3.2 Bidirectional Spatiotemporal Decoder:
To extract bimanual information from the feature grid, 48 queries per frame are deployed: 2 hand tokens (left and right), 42 joint tokens (21 per hand), and 4 register tokens. Each joint query probabilistically grounds to 2D anchor positions via spatial cross-attention, while temporal non-causal (bidirectional) self-attention with Rotary position embeddings integrates context across all frames. Because physical hand size remains constant in egocentric video, a Shape Head temporally pools hand tokens across the entire clip to predict the hand shape parameter $\hat{\beta}$ once, preventing temporal shape jitter.

3.3 Ray-Based Camera Solver:
To remove dependence on camera intrinsics, a Ray Head predicts the viewing ray direction $\hat{r}$ for each spatial cell from the latent features. For 3D translation, a hybrid Perspective-n-Point (PnP) approach is adopted. The network only regresses depth $\hat{t}_z = \exp(\hat{\zeta})$, while in-plane translation $(t_x, t_y)$ is solved algebraically via weighted least squares using predicted 2D joint anchors and viewing rays. This allows highly accurate metric 3D placement even when camera calibration is unavailable at test time (K-free).

captions.F3: Architecture of the Bidirectional Spatiotemporal Decoder. Spatial Cross-Attention and temporal Self-Attention alternate across 4 layers to output MANO parameters through joint, pose, and camera heads. Predicted viewing rays (Ray PE) are injected as geometric cues, enabling the PnP solver to recover accurate 3D translation without camera intrinsics.

sections.heading: Exceptional accuracy and real-time speed overcoming occlusions and out-of-sight exits
sections.summary: Evaluated against 10 baselines across 5 benchmarks including ARCTIC, HOT3D, and HOI4D, ACE-Ego-Hand achieved SOTA on 45 out of 48 primary metrics. Recovery accuracy for out-of-sight hands improved dramatically, all while reaching an inference speed of 63 fps.
sections.details:
4.1 Experimental Setup:
Training was conducted on a mixture of egocentric video datasets such as ARCTIC, HOT3D, H2O, and OakInk2, along with synthetic renders and single-image datasets. HOI4D was held out for zero-shot evaluation. Evaluation metrics include Procrustes-aligned 3D joint error (MPJPE-p), metrics with missed-detection penalties, and error metrics that include out-of-sight hands (MPJPE +OOS).

4.2 Main Results:
For visible hands in-frame, ACE-Ego-Hand reduced MPJPE-p compared to previous state-of-the-art ViDiHand by 30% on ARCTIC (21.67 mm → 15.26 mm), 40% on wide-angle HOT3D (21.51 mm → 12.89 mm), and 23% on zero-shot HOI4D. Detection F1 scores also reached near-saturation levels. Moreover, the calibration-free "K-free" setting maintained accuracy nearly identical to the calibrated configuration.
The out-of-sight (OOS) recovery performance was particularly striking. On evaluation including OOS hands (MPJPE +OOS), errors dropped by 45.9% on ARCTIC and 61.1% on HOT3D relative to ViDiHand. Evaluating purely on out-of-sight frames (MPJPE OOS) yielded errors of around 35 to 38 mm, far outperforming existing methods that degraded to 120–150 mm.
Inference speed reached 63.1 fps on a single A100 GPU, roughly 33× faster than ViDiHand (1.91 fps).

4.3 Ablation Studies:
In comparisons of video backbones (Table 2), using the Wan 2.2 diffusion model (16.95 mm) halved the error compared to raw RGB inputs (46.50 mm) and VAE latents (32.50 mm). Replacing the backbone with self-supervised V-JEPA 2 preserved in-frame accuracy, but out-of-sight error (MPJPE OOS) degraded significantly from 41.5 mm to 66.1 mm. This confirms that spatiotemporal dynamics learned through generative pretraining are uniquely powerful for predicting unseen hands.

captions.F4: Qualitative comparison on ARCTIC (top) and HOT3D (bottom). While existing methods lose track of a hand during occlusions or suffer from severe wrist trajectory jitter, the proposed method (Ours) maintains smooth, ground-truth-aligned 3D trajectories even through heavy hand-hand overlap and out-of-sight frame exits.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook
sections.summary: Repurposing a diffusion model as a deterministic geometry encoder enables fast, occlusion-robust 3D hand tracking. Its offline design that leverages full-clip context provides a scalable foundation for generating massive robot manipulation datasets.
sections.details:
This work introduces ACE-Ego-Hand, a new paradigm that repurposes video diffusion models as single-pass geometry encoders rather than multi-step image renderers. By coupling a bidirectional spatiotemporal decoder with a ray-based camera solver, it achieves unprecedented robustness to occlusions and temporary out-of-sight gaps while drastically reducing computational overhead.

These results provide a strong bridge for converting massive collections of human egocentric activity videos into high-quality manipulation trajectories that robots can learn via imitation.

Current limitations include reduced generalization of predicted viewing rays to camera optics (such as field of view) outside the training distribution, as well as the requirement for offline full-clip processing. Future work discusses distilling the framework into causal streaming models for real-time, closed-loop robot control.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details, long video generalization, and robot retargeting
sections.summary: The appendix details sequence-length generalization via Rotary position embeddings, camera fitting behavior near image borders without intrinsics, and retargeting reconstructed bimanual trajectories to an Inspire Hand multi-fingered robot hand.
sections.details:
- Speed vs. Accuracy Trade-off (Figure F5):
Comparing average 3D error across benchmarks against inference speed shows that ACE-Ego-Hand outperforms previous top-performing methods by a wide margin while running above 60 fps, demonstrating clear Pareto dominance.

- Camera Fitting Effects at Image Margins:
In the K-free configuration without camera intrinsics, directly querying viewing rays near image borders incurs high angular uncertainty, leading to large translation errors. The closed-form camera fitting step in this method effectively suppresses translation errors for hands at the periphery or outside the frame.

- Generalization to Clip Length and Tap Depth:
Because temporal attention employs Rotary relative position embeddings, the model can decode full video sequences (hundreds to over 1000 frames) in a single pass beyond the 81 frames seen during training. Experiments also show that tapping intermediate features at block 15 preserves the expressive power of the full network while saving substantial compute.

- Robot Hand Retargeting (Figure F9):
Joint angles computed from metric 3D hand joints were mapped onto an Inspire Hand multi-fingered robot hand. Complex tool use and object manipulation from videos were reproduced smoothly and synchronously on the robot hand, confirming practical utility as a data generation pipeline for robot imitation learning.

captions.F5: Comparison of accuracy and inference speed (Figure S1). The vertical axis shows MPJPE-p error (lower is better), and the horizontal axis shows frames per second on a single A100 (FPS, log scale). Our method (star) substantially sets a new state of the art while running at a fast 63 fps.
captions.F9: Example of retargeting egocentric video to a robot hand (Figure S6). Showing input RGB (left), hand mesh recovered by ACE-Ego-Hand (center), and retargeting result on the Inspire Hand (right). Fine finger articulation is mapped to the robot with high fidelity.

takeaways: Even without iterative denoising sampling, features from a single forward pass over clean latents in video diffusion models carry rich physical and spatiotemporal priors.
For reconstructing unseen hands (out of sight or occluded), generative pretrained models offer superior predictive capability compared to discriminative self-supervised models like V-JEPA.
Predicting viewing rays from latent features and solving via PnP enables metric 3D hand placement even when camera intrinsics are completely unknown at test time.
Processing the bidirectional context of an entire clip at once fundamentally avoids the drift and tracking loss inherent in per-frame detectors and causal trackers.
limitations: Because the architecture is designed for offline processing across an entire clip, it cannot be directly used for real-time closed-loop robot control without modifications (it is targeted at dataset preprocessing and imitation learning).

Accuracy improvements for out-of-sight (OOS) hands were primarily verified on Procrustes-aligned joint poses (MPJPE OOS); absolute depth and translation guarantees without visual evidence still carry inherent uncertainty.
The calibration-free solver assumes pinhole geometry for its linear regression formulation, which can degrade in accuracy on cameras with extreme non-linear distortion, such as fisheye lenses.
